title: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS”—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU START READING ONE VERSE EARLIER?
paragraphs: “WIVES, SUBMIT TO YOUR HUSBANDS”—BUT WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU START READING ONE VERSE EARLIER?
The verse that has started arguments, wounded marriages, been weaponized by controlling men, rejected by wounded women—and sometimes quoted without the sentence that comes immediately before it.
There are Bible verses people whisper when they are hurting.
And there are Bible verses people shout when they want to win.
Ephesians 5:22 has sometimes become the second kind.
“Wives, submit to your own husbands…”
Some women hear those words and feel peace because they have seen biblical marriage lived beautifully.
Others hear them and their stomach tightens.
Because somebody once used those words against them.
Maybe a husband quoted “submission” while refusing correction.
Maybe a pastor told her to endure what should never have been called godly.
Maybe a man demanded obedience while giving very little resemblance to Jesus.
And maybe somewhere along the way, she quietly began wondering…
Is this really what God intended?
But there is something painfully important we need to notice.
Before Paul speaks directly to wives…
before he tells husbands how to love…
before we build an entire theology of marriage from verse 22…
there is verse 21.
And once you see it, you cannot pretend it isn't there.
The Greek reads:
“ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ”
hypotassomenoi allēlois en phobō Christou.
“Submitting to one another in the fear [or reverence] of Christ.”
That is Ephesians 5:21.
And the grammatical connection matters.
Paul's thought did not originally arrive with modern chapter headings, paragraph titles, bold print, or verse numbers separating verse 21 from verse 22.

Even more striking, significant early Greek witnesses of Ephesians 5:22 contain no independently expressed verb for “submit” in verse 22; the idea is supplied from the preceding context. Other manuscripts contain an explicit form of the verb, which is why careful textual discussion matters.
Either way, verse 21 and verse 22 are not strangers living on opposite sides of a theological wall.
They belong to the same flow of thought.
And the flow begins even earlier.
Paul has been describing what Spirit-filled Christian life looks like.
“Be filled with the Spirit…”
Then come speaking, singing, thanksgiving…
and submission.
Not domination.
Not ego.
Not “How much authority can I exercise?”
But a community increasingly transformed by Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the marriage passage begins to feel different.
Not because “wives, submit” disappears.
It doesn't.
We do not honor Scripture by erasing words that make modern people uncomfortable.
But neither do we honor Scripture by isolating words that make controlling people comfortable.
Read the whole passage.
The wife is addressed.
Then the husband is addressed.
And what does Paul tell the husband?
“Husbands, love your wives…”
That sounds gentle enough until you keep reading.
“…as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Read that again.
Gave.
Himself.
Up.
Paul does not hand the Christian husband a throne.
He points him toward a cross.
The standard is not, “Make sure she knows who's boss.”
The standard is Christ.
The Christ who washed feet.
The Christ who welcomed the broken.
The Christ who touched people society avoided.
The Christ who laid aside privilege.
The Christ who endured nails.
The Christ who bled.
The Christ who gave Himself for His bride.
So before any Christian husband pounds his fist on the table demanding, “Submit to me,” perhaps he should first look toward Calvary and hear another question:
Are you loving her like THAT?
Because biblical headship can never legitimately become permission for cruelty.
Christ does not brutalize His bride.
Christ does not humiliate His bride for entertainment.
Christ does not manipulate His bride to protect His ego.
Christ does not use Scripture as a weapon to make His bride afraid of Him.
He gives Himself for her.
And that changes everything.
The Greek word translated “submit” in verse 21 comes from ὑποτάσσω—hypotassō.
But whatever debates Christians may have about the precise implications of that word for marital roles, one fact cannot be escaped:
Paul places the entire discussion under allegiance to Christ.
The marriage is not ultimately about the supremacy of the husband.
It is not ultimately about the independence of the wife.
It is about Jesus.
That is why Christian marriage cannot simply become a baptized version of a power struggle.
The Gospel invades the home.
Pride meets the cross.
Selfishness meets the cross.
Control meets the cross.
Bitterness meets the cross.
Entitlement meets the cross.
The wife belongs to Jesus before she belongs to her husband.
The husband belongs to Jesus before he exercises any responsibility toward his wife.
Both stand beneath the lordship of Christ.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need forgiveness.
Both need the Holy Spirit.
And both will eventually discover something uncomfortable:
The greatest enemy inside many marriages isn't sitting on the opposite side of the bed.
It is the sin still fighting for control inside both human hearts.
That is why this passage cannot merely become ammunition for gender arguments.
It is supposed to become a mirror.
Husband…
when was the last time you apologized without defending yourself?
When was the last time you sacrificed something you genuinely wanted because loving your wife mattered more?
When was the last time she felt emotionally safe enough to tell you that you hurt her?
When was the last time you asked whether your “leadership” actually resembles the crucified Savior you claim to follow?
And wife…
has disappointment slowly hardened into contempt?
Have years of hurt made respect almost impossible?
Have you begun punishing him emotionally for wounds you have never honestly brought into the light?
Are you asking Jesus to transform your marriage while quietly refusing to let Him transform you?
Those questions sting.
They are supposed to.
Not because Christianity is trying to crush us…
but because Jesus loves us too much to leave our hidden idols untouched.
And sometimes the idol is control.
Sometimes it is pride.
Sometimes it is being right.
Sometimes it is being obeyed.
Sometimes it is refusing to forgive.
Sometimes it is maintaining the appearance of a Christian marriage while two people are spiritually bleeding behind a closed door.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Not inside a theological debate.
Inside a hurting marriage.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still attend church.
You still smile.
You still upload the anniversary photo.
People comment, “Beautiful couple!”
And you stare at those words knowing how quiet the drive home was.
Knowing what was said last night.
Knowing how long it has been since either of you felt truly seen.
Maybe your marriage isn't collapsing dramatically.
Maybe it is dying politely.
One unanswered wound at a time.
One sarcastic remark.
One withheld apology.
One night facing opposite directions.
One more prayer neither of you prayed together.
And somehow you became roommates carrying wedding rings.
Please hear this:
Jesus is not intimidated by what your marriage has become.
The same Gospel that raises spiritually dead sinners can enter rooms where love seems dead too.
That does not mean every story becomes easy.
It does not mean reconciliation can be forced by one spouse.
And it absolutely does not mean a person experiencing abuse should silently endure danger because someone quoted the word “submit.”
Sin should not be renamed submission.
Coercion should not be renamed leadership.
Fear should not be renamed respect.
And protecting someone from genuine harm is not rebellion against Jesus.
The biblical picture is infinitely more beautiful than that.
Paul eventually reaches Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Then he says something astonishing.
This mystery is profound…
and he is speaking about Christ and the church.
There it is.
The secret beneath the marriage passage.
Jesus.
Christian marriage points beyond itself.
A husband and wife are sinners standing inside a living picture of something far greater than themselves—the covenant love of Christ for His people.
That is why marriage exposes us so deeply.
Marriage eventually introduces another human being to versions of you the church crowd never sees.
They see the worshipper.
Your spouse sees the temper.
They see the Bible verse you posted.
Your spouse heard the sentence you wish you could take back.
They see the ministry.
Your spouse sees whether the Gospel reaches the kitchen.
They see your Sunday clothes.
Your spouse sees Monday night.
And perhaps that is where real discipleship begins.
Not when everybody thinks you're spiritual.
But when Jesus is allowed into the places where nobody is applauding.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter failed Jesus publicly.
David's sin brought devastation.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated history.
Paul himself had persecuted the church.
Scripture is filled with human beings whose stories could have ended at their worst chapter.
But Jesus has always been in the business of rewriting stories.
Not by pretending sin never happened.
By confronting it.
Forgiving it.
Redeeming sinners from it.
And transforming those who surrender to Him.
That is grace.
Grace does not say, “It doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “It mattered enough for Jesus to bleed for it.”
The cross simultaneously tells us how terrible sin is and how astonishing God's mercy is.
So maybe the question after reading Ephesians 5 should not merely be:
“Who is supposed to submit?”
Maybe another necessary question is:
“Where have I refused to become like Jesus?”
Because you can win the argument about marriage and still lose your marriage to pride.
You can memorize Ephesians 5 and never imitate Ephesians 5.
You can demand biblical order while living with an unbiblical heart.
You can insist that somebody fulfill their role while quietly refusing the cross-shaped responsibilities Scripture gives you.
And Jesus is after something deeper than outward compliance.
He wants hearts.
Husbands surrendered to Christ.
Wives surrendered to Christ.
Homes surrendered to Christ.
Pride surrendered to Christ.
Sexuality surrendered to Christ.
Money surrendered to Christ.
Arguments surrendered to Christ.
Trauma brought honestly before Christ.
Sin confessed before Christ.
Forgiveness received through Christ.
Because Christianity is not ultimately behavior management.
It is resurrection.
Maybe your marriage needs counseling.
Get help.
Maybe you owe someone an apology.
Give it without excuses.
Maybe you have been controlling.
Repent.
Maybe you have become cruel.
Repent.
Maybe bitterness has become your emotional shelter.
Bring it to Jesus.
Maybe there is serious abuse or danger.
Seek safety and trustworthy pastoral, professional, and—when necessary—legal help. No interpretation of Ephesians 5 requires someone to cooperate with violence or conceal criminal behavior.
And maybe you are reading this unmarried.
Because Ephesians 5 is exposing something bigger than marriage.
Every Christian is being called away from self-rule and toward Christ.
“Submitting to one another in the fear of Christ.”
Imagine churches shaped by that.
Imagine marriages shaped by that.
Imagine men who measure strength by how much of themselves they can sacrificially give rather than how much control they can obtain.
Imagine women cherished rather than silenced.
Imagine disagreements where winning matters less than holiness.
Imagine children growing up watching Daddy apologize.
Watching Mommy forgive.
Watching both parents kneel before Jesus.
Not perfection.
Repentance.
Not performance.
Grace.
Not pretending wounds don't exist.
Healing.
That is the home the Gospel begins creating when Jesus becomes more than decoration on the wall and actually becomes Lord of the people living beneath that roof.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs this tonight.
And if this exposed something in your own heart, don't hide behind a reaction button.
And if you are not comfortable telling your story publicly, simply comment, “Jesus, have Your way.”
There is no shame in admitting you need grace.
The entire Christian faith begins with people admitting exactly that.
Because there may come a night after an argument when you need to read it again—not to find ammunition against your spouse, but to remember the cross.
It doesn't.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never could.
Salvation is by God's grace.
And your local church, its needs, and your convictions about biblical giving should not be casually displaced by an online ministry.
But voluntary support of Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of participating in work you believe is bearing spiritual fruit.
If you want to glorify God through supporting this particular work, you can do so freely and prayerfully—not under pressure, but as an act of willing generosity.
Send it privately to the couple nobody realizes is struggling.
Pray for this ministry.
Help truth travel farther than an algorithm would naturally carry it.
Because somewhere tonight a woman may be wondering whether Christianity requires her to disappear.
Somewhere a husband may finally realize that biblical leadership looks much more like dying to himself than demanding his way.
Somewhere a couple may be one honest conversation away from asking for help.
Somewhere someone has heard Ephesians 5:22 shouted at them for years…
and desperately needs to discover the Christ whose cross stands over the entire passage.
So read verse 22.
Believe verse 22.
But don't amputate it from verse 21.
And don't stop before verse 25.
Keep reading until the husband meets the cross.
Keep reading until husband and wife meet Christ.
Keep reading until authority loses its appetite for domination.
Keep reading until submission cannot be confused with enabling evil.
Keep reading until marriage becomes something larger than two people fighting for control.
Keep reading until you reach the mystery.
Christ.
And His church.
The Bridegroom who did not save His bride by overpowering her…
but by giving Himself for her.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody needs to carry into their marriage tonight:
Before you use Scripture to ask what your spouse owes you, stand beneath the cross and ask Jesus what love requires of you.
That question could change an argument.
It could change a marriage.
It could change a family.
And by the grace of Christ…
it could change generations.
Because the Gospel does not merely tell wives to submit or husbands to love.
The Gospel brings proud, wounded, sinful human beings to the feet of a crucified and risen King…
until both finally realize that Jesus was never asking them to use Scripture to conquer each other.
He was calling them to belong completely to Him.
And when Jesus becomes Lord of the home, the goal is no longer to determine who can force the other person lower.
The question becomes who is willing to kneel before Christ.
Remember this when the argument starts again:
The safest marriage is not one where somebody finally wins the war for control—it is one where two sinners keep surrendering the throne to Jesus.
